text:
“New Waters Near La Paz Promise Prolific Supply of Sea Food. 
 Competition In the Lower California fisheries trade, advocated by the California state game and fish commission as a means of crating a supply greater than the demand, and therefore resulting in the lowering of the high cost of living, is beginning to bear fruit. 
 For years fishermen operating out of this port have been compelled to pay tribute to certain concessional holders of fishing rights along the southern littoral for the privilege of operating in those waters. 
 Independent fishermen, headed by M. Kondo, have now started fishing in waters south of the twenty eighth parallel under permits granted by the governor of La Paz. These waters form a prolific source of supply of halibut, barracuda, lobsters and other kinds of shellfish. 
 Two California inspectors have been commissioned to go south with the lobster craft operating under permits issued by the governor of La Paz. These officers are being paid by the importers, as required by law. Their duties are to certify that the provisions of the California law governing lobster importation are respected. A third inspector will arrive here April 10. 
 In addition to granting permits overriding the concessionaires operating for the Cantu government, the Mexican de facto government as represented in the La Paz regime has taken the California fish and game laws for its guidance in conserving the west Mexican fisheries and has appointed its own inspectors to accompany the boats to which it has issued permits, to see that the fishing craft take no young fish, use no trawl nets or other gear destructive of the future supply. 
 Work of the concessionaires under this new competitive arrangement, fostered by the simplifying of importation under rulings of the fish and game commission, will extend to the fresh fish trade within a short time. Owing to the distance traveled refrigerating apparatus will have to be installed on boats operating to the new fishing grounds in the vicinity of Turtle and Magdalena bays. 
 The auxiliary schooners None Such and Telemaches are now operating exclusively between this port and Turtle bay in the lobster and turtle carrying trade. Turtle meat now is being sold at 8 cents a pound In the California markets, and the demand is said to be far greater than the supply. 
 Captain Robert Israel, who, with Kondo, is establishing an independent lobster and turtle trade at this port, and who is operating the None Such and Telemaches, plans to put another vessel in service between here and Turtle bay within a few weeks. 
 The floating cannery John A. Heston is operating at Magdalena bay, engaged in the canning of turtle soup, sardines and other fish products. The Heston, during the tuna season, is expected to pack thousands of cases of this delectable sea food for shipment to San Diego, thence to be distributed to the Southern California, Western and Eastern markets. 
 Five thousand pounds of halibut and barracuda arrived in port yesterday from the halibut banks north of Cedros on the fishing schooner Josephine Z.”
headline: "PUBLIC TO BENEFIT FROM OPENING OF FISHING GROUNDS"
notes: "location is not specified to an individual fishing site, but instead clarifies that fishing is 'south of the 28th parallel' and includes Magdalena bay, turtle bay, and La Paz"

text:
"W. W. Beach, of 437 North Mesa street, has been experimenting for some years in canning various kinds of crustaceans and other sea animal life, and has now hit upon what he thinks will be one of the most highly priced delicacies every placed on the market. The product is called “turtle stock,” and consists of Calipash, Calipee and other edible parts of the green turtle, put up In a concentrated form for the making of turtle soup. 
 Enormous numbers of these green turtles have been brought up from Magdalena and Turtle bays for years past and sold alive in the Los Angeles and San Francisco markets. This is probably the first successful method of canning the turtle so that it can be placed on the market in a practicable and preserved form. 
 The formula states that the soup should contain besides the one pound can of turtle stock, one pound of carrots, one pound of ham, 1/2 pound of veal, 1/2 pound of onions, 2 eggs, hard-boiled, 1/2 lemon, 2 pounds of tomatoes, strained, 1 large glass of port, sherry or maideria wine, 1 large tablespoonful of beef drippings, 1 tablespoonful of Cury. This will make one gallon of the most delicious turtle soup, enough for sixteen people, which will keep for several days, if reheated once in forty-eight hours. 
 Mr. Beach has arranged to have the turtles brought here in local boats and the product will be put up by the White Star Canning Co., at East San Pedro. It is thought that the possibilities of the industry are large and that one more form of food has been wrested from the mysteries of the great Pacific ocean, lying practically unexplored and teeming with many forms of life which may yet go far toward solving the problem of supplying the ever increasing demand for something new in food stuffs."
headline: "WILL PACK TURTLES AT WHITE STAR"
notes: "This is connected to sppilot_19190319. This is not a reporting of a specific cargo shipment/capture, nor is it for one particular time. It merely claims that there were consistent shipments of these turtles over the years to fuel the canning industry. Additionally, it cites both magdalena and turtle bays as locations, hence the two labels for location"

text: "It is a singular fact that turtle is appreciated in California neither as an article of food nor an element of commerce. Californians can hardly be persuaded to eat turtle. In New York, and the East generally, and over the whole world, turtle is regarded as a great delicacy. [Captain Bogart] informed me that turtle exist in wonderful quantities on the Lower California coast. It may be impossible to make a market for the dainty in California, but the meat can be packed and exported. Captain Bogart informs us that Scammon’s Lagoon, several lagoons to the north of it, and the bay at Cerros [Cedros] Island are crammed with turtle. Many sloughs open into the lagoons, and the practice of the turtle is to float up them at flood-tide and feed. Captain Bogart, by stretching a seine over the mouth of these sloughs, has captured eight tons at a single haul. He could have taken more but had no room for them.”

text: "TURTLE BAY TURTLE DISAPPEARS Speaking of Turtle bay, the shelled animal from which it gained its name because of the great numbers of turtles there in the early days, is now to be found there but rarely. The advancing front line of civilization and appetites for soup have driven the turtle to his last stronghold, farther down the Mexican coast. San Pedro fishermen cruising down the coast occasionally capture one of the large creatures. One such turtle brought back to the municipal fish wharf alive some time ago had laid a peck of eggs on the trip. Capture of one of the turtles is always an occasion for celebration by the fishermen. The heavy fishing in Turtle bay is believed to have caused the animals to leave."
headline: "FISH PACKERS MARKING TIME"
notes: "While this article mentions the capture of one turtle, it is predominantly about the ABSENCE of many turtles in Turtle bay as they once were. The single turtle captured was a marked rarity. This demonstrates a change in the cargo-yielding capacity of Baja California."

"E. R. Kline Lands Rare Species Weighing 800 Pounds After Three Hours' Struggle. 
 After fighting desperately for over three hours to regain its freedom an immense royal sea turtle was landed at the La Jolla bath house yesterday afternoon about 4 o'clock by K. B. Kline, who caught the big fellow in the cove near Del Mar. Although not placed on the scales it was estimated that the turtle would weigh at least 800 pounds. 
 Kline was out in a small boat when he noticed the turtle asleep in the kelp near Del Mar. Approaching the sleeping denizen of the deep he succeeded in sinking his spear into its body. Then began the struggle between man and turtle, which only ended some three hours later when Kline landed his trophy at La Jolla. 
 The turtle, owing to its immense size and particular species, was taken to the biological station for purposes of study. There it was cattalogued as a loggerhead, which, while infesting the Pacific, are seldom found so close inshore. The turtle measured more than six feet in length, with immense flippers, like a seal; a head larger than a man's head and powerful jaws."
headline: "Mammoth Turtle Makes Desperate Fight For Liberty"

text:
"Reptile Believed to Have Swam to These Waters From The Indies 
 J. Preoata, Roy Edwards. J. Rodriguez, W. Westfall, D. Tann and C. Pruett, fishermen in the employ of the San Diego Fish company, yesterday captured what is believed to be the largest turtle ever caught in this vicinity. The men were engaged in fishing on the western banks; about five miles southwest of the Coronado islands, when a member of the party sighted the monster, which, when they finally landed it at the dock after a seven hour struggle, weighed 2500 pounds. 
 The reptile measured 7 feet 2 inches from the tip of its nose to tip of tall, was 5 feet 2 inches wide and 2 feet thick. The liver weighed 100 pounds, and the shell, after it had been cleaned and scraped, weighed a trifle over 200 pounds. According to Edwards, who kept the shell as a souvenir, the turtle put up a terrific fight before it was finally landed. A steel harpoon was broken in the first attempt to kill the reptile. The men then determined to take a half hitch with a hawser around the monster's fins and tow it in port. This they finally succeeded in accomplishing, after a seven-hour-fight In which it broke away from its captors three times. The men repeatedly had to gaff the turtle in order to replace the line over its flippers. 
 It is believed the turtle came from the Indies, taking several years to make the trip. The shell is not similar to those found on the species which frequent the Galapagos Islands and which are noted for their size. The reptile also had the pointed nose which is characteristic of the Indian turtle. 
 The fishermen killed their game soon after it was landed at the San Diego Fishing company's wharf at the foot of D street and the meat put in cold storage. According to the captors the turtle was disporting with a small whale when it was first sighted by them."
headline: "Turtle Weighing 2500 Pounds Is Captured After 7-Hour Struggle"
notes: "also noted the width and thickness as 5'2" and 2 feet, respectively. Species was not identified so assumed green, but if the size was indeed so large this seems unlikely. Additionally, even if this were a leatherback, 2500 lbs seems too high."

text:
"Turtle Caught by Steve Zolezzie While He Was Fishing in Ocean South of San Diego. 
 Ocean-Going Monster Weighing 487 Pounds Becomes Entangled in Net 
 A giant green turtle which became entangled in nets of Steve Zolezzi, a local fisherman, was captured by him and a companion in the kelp near the boundary line yesterday morning. 
 The big chelonian was found about 5 o'clock, when the fishermen went out to pay their usual morning visit to their nets. It had completely enmeshed itself and its captor worked hard for several hours before it was finally freed and the nets were hauled away from its vicious back-shaped jaws. One section of the nets was practically destroyed, involving a loss of about$50 to the owners. 
 Despite the enormous size of the turtle it was finally dragged into Zolezzi’s boat by the fisherman and his companion and brought to San Diego. It was landed at the wharf of the San Diego fish market, where it was the cynosure of curious eyes during the entire day. It will not be killed until Monday, when, according to the statements of the market management last night, the edible portions of its huge hulk will be sold to Harry Rudder of the Union cafe. 
 The turtle tipped the scales at 487 pounds."
headline: "GIANT TURTLE ENTRAPPED; SOON TO BE IN THE SOUP"

notes: "note that the name of the man who caught turtle is spelled two different ways (typo). While 487 lbs seems perhaps unrealistically heavy, it is an exact weight reported to be measured by scales, not an estimate."

text:
"Monster Found By Fisherman Off Coast Evidently In Toils Before 
 HAS NAME AND DATE BURNED IN SHELL 
 Evidently Picked Up By British Ship Sea Bride in August 1881 
 Of all the peculiar and mysterious things given up by the sea, one of the most puzzling ever found by San Diego fishermen was discovered yesterday in the shape of a gigantic turtle captured in a fish net by Julius Solissa, who is considered the cleverest fisherman in the city, despite his youth. 
 Solissa, who is employed by Charles Holmquist, president of the San Diego Fish company, went out in his big gasoline fishing launch to the cod banks on his regular trip last Wednesday morning at 1:30 o'clock. Nothing out of the ordinary routine of fishing occurred, as the running was slow and poor for hours. 
 Young Solissa's trained eye soon discovered that something was wrong with the nets and the disturbance suddenly grew, so that it appeared as though some monster were churning the water under the boat. 
 Solissa believed at first that some of the seals which patrol the nets in big herds had become entangled in the nets and nettled back to wait until they had been drowned by being held under the water for a long time. 
 But the row continued and Solissa finally concluding that a large fish must be the cause of the trouble proceeded to drag in the nets to look them over. 
 He was greatly surprised to find an enormous turtle, which struggled so violently that it wound the strings of the net around its flippers and cut them until the blood ran and the flesh was torn to shreds. 
 Solissa lowered the net and made off to find his mates in the other launches. Returning, three other fishermen aided Julius to' make the turtle fast to the boat, but it was all they could do to handle it, as the turtle pulled them around like mere children. They were finally compelled to give up the task of pulling the turtle into the boat, and were satisfied to tow it in with them on Thursday noon. 
 When the turtle was finally landed in the shipping room of the San Diego Fish company, the big surprise came. 
 Although the monster's back shell was covered with slime and barnacles, when these were scraped off and the shell fairly cleaned, numerous characters were plainly visible. It appeared that they had been either burned or cut deep into the shell years ago. 
 After some study, the following inscription was deciphered: 
 “Br. S. Sea Bride —Aug. 12, 1881—3S.—86 W." was on the left side of the turtle's shell, looking toward the head, while these words were on the right side: 
 "If Found Please Notify— Thomas Fletcher—Brawley Road. Rivington, Eng.” 
 It would appear from an Interpretation of the inscription that a sailor or officer of the British ship Sea Bride, caught this turtle in Pacific waters off the coast of South America, August 12, 1881, in latitude 3 South and longitude 86 west, branded or cut the characters indicated on the turtle's shell and threw it back into the ocean again. 
 The turtle must, therefore, he at least 26 years old, and it is probable that it is much older, as it tipped the scales at 1,902 1-2 pounds—nearly a ton— while it measured 5 feet 2 inches over the shell from front to rear. 
 It was wrinkled about the neck like a clown's collar and was a pathetic sight as it lay on the shipping room floor, helpless as a baby, its great flippers all torn to pieces by its own futile struggles in the fishing net. 
 The turtle was immediately sold by evidently quite wary and wise to have escaped the wiles of man and its fellow monsters of the deep for over 26 years, but its feminine curiosity for the fishing net probably caused its capture an ddeath. 
 The turtle was immediately sold by telegraphic order to a big fish market in Los Angeles and by this time is probably nothing but fine French soup and steaks on the fashionable tables of that city.”

text: "A large leather back sea turtle was caught recently by the Ressiean brothers and was taken to George Kline, biologist at La Jolla. It was harpooned in the kelp fields off the Coronado Islands. The turtle is one of the largest on record, weighing 1570 pounds. \n It is 11 feet from tip to tip, has a head like a walrus, two distinct tails and a soft, fur-llke body. There are seven ribs running lengthwise of the body. The leather back is almost extinct now, having been hunted out in years past for the blubber, that was used for medicinal purposes."

text:
“W. J. Forbes Hooks Huge Turtle Which Carries Boat to Sea; Capsizes 
 Word has been received from Lower California that William J. Forbes, prominent in the affairs of Wall street while thousands of miles removed from the financial disturbance of the eastern metropolis, had a close call the other day from drowning in the waters of Todos Santos bay, thirty or forty miles south of Ensenada. 
 Forbes, who has a number of warm friends in San Diego, is the guest of Walter Nordhoff, who owns a splendid country home on the shores of the bay, and who is famous as an entertainer. The Wall street financier was out fishing from a small boat, accompanied by a boatman, when a huge turtle was hooked. Forbes was unable to land the fish, and within a short time they were off for a cruise, the destination of which they knew not. It was worse than sailing under sealed orders in that there was no certainty that the destination would ever be known. 
 However, after the turtle had towed them for an hour or two the men in the boat, becoming exasperated, resolved to either land the fish or overturn the boat in the attempt. The effort resulted in the capsizing of the craft. 
 In the advices received here nothing is said about the boatman, and it is supposed that he was more fortunate than Forbes, who was in the water nearly two hours before the rescue. 
 Local friends are awaiting the full details of the accident.”
headline: "NEW YORK BANKER NEARLY DROWNS"

text: "SPEARING deep sea fish as they swim into the bays of the coast line is one of the most fascinating branches of piscatorial sport. It requires an expert to hurl the harpoon into the bodies of the great fish as they fash by, many feet under water, but Paul of Ocean Beach is a real expert in this difficult art. Young Paul, poised on the bridge over the entrance to Mission bay, successfully harpooned a giant black bass or Jewfish, weighing 275 pounds. Young Paul and his prize are shown in the accompanying picture. \n At the lower left of the photograph is the shell of a giant sea turtle, also harpooned by Paul several days previous to his capture of the big fish. The turtle weighed almost 300 pounds and was caught by Paul with the aid of A. W. Brand of the Mission bath house, who also assisted in landing the giant fish."
headline: "Giant Bass Speared From Mission Bridge"

text: "The steamer National City, Capt. J. D. Higgins, arrived in port yesterday from San Pedro and discharged a portion of her cargo of lumber at the Western Lumber company’s wharf, proceeding on to the Russ wharf, where she is now completing unloading. \n The steam schooner Bernardo Reyes arrived in port yesterday afternoon from Ensenada, members of her crew bringing with them the report of the capture of a monster turtle en route. The turtle weighed in the neighborhood of 1999 pounds, it is alleged, and was speared as it lay asleep. Upon being hauled to the deck it was found to have six large ridges of fin-like material on its back, according to the statements of a member of the crew, a neck as large around as a man’s, and two semi-tusks protruding from its mouth. It measured over five feet from head to tail, it is asserted. The turtle died on the way here and was thrown overboard, said the captain of the Bernardo Reyes, hence the statements of the crew will have to be accepted as to the size and species of the monster of the deep."
headline: "WATERFRONT AND SHIPPING NEWS"

text: "An immense turtle arrived in this city yesterday over the Santa Fe from San Diego. It was captured off the coast of Lower California by the crew of a tramp steamer.\n The turtle was purchased by the Zalser Produce company of this city, and when the bill of lading was made out in San Diego, the turtle weighed 325 pounds. It barely tipped the scales at 310 pounds yesterday afternoon, the loss being caused by the hot weather and absence of the several buckets of salt water with which it was doused many times a day on ship board. \n Nevertheless his turtleship was able to crawl around at a lively rate when disturbed. When the turtle ceases to exist genuine turtle soup will be obtainable at several of the downtown restaurants."

text:
“CAPTURED IN WATERS NEAR SANTA BARBARA 
 Creature Measures Seven Feet From Head to Tall and Its Weight Is Eight Hundred Pounds 
 Special to The Herald. 
 SANTA BARBARA, Jan. 4.— Captain Gourley of the pleasure fleet and one of his assistants, Albert Stafford, captured a huge sea turtle yesterday afternoon which proved to be the largest specimen ever caught in these waters. When hauled onto the pleasure pier and carefully anchored down with stout ropes to prevent trouble it was estimated that the turtle weighed at least 800 pounds, and several competent judges placed its weight at considerably above this figure. 
 The turtle was first discovered by Stafford, who came across it while rowing alone in a small skiff. The reptile was entangled in some kelp, and was asleep at the time Stafford sighted it. Not liking to venture too near in so small a boat, Stafford returned and was joined by Gourley. The pair went after the turtle in a sail boat and succeeded in gaffing it through one of the flippers, after which they managed to throw ropes over it and tow it to the pier. The turtle put up a hard fight all the way and several times attempted to clamber aboard the boat. It was finally hoisted to the pier, after a few exciting moments for those who were engaged in the work. 
 The picture was taken within a few minutes of the time the big turtle was finally made fast to the pier. The turtle measured seven feet from head to tail.”
headline: "MONSTER TURTLE TAKEN PRISONER"
notes: "I thought it would be a leatherback based on the image and the descriptions of size, but unsure. Location just generally says 'near Santa Barbara"

text:
“1200-Pounder Is Named for President 
 (Special to The Herald.) 
 SAN PEDRO. May 6.—"Teddy Roosevelt," a 1200-pound turtle, which was caught yesterday by Capt. George Evitch twelve miles off the coast, is to go to the St. Louis exposition. Hundreds of people took a look at the monster today. As soon as arrangements can be made it will be sent east by rail. 
 The turtle measures seven feet in length and is four feet wide. From tip to tip of his flippers the distance is about ten feet. It has the appearance of being several hundred years old. Three ridges run lengthwise on the shell. 
 Several bullet holes are records of previous ineffectual attempts at his capture. The shell is of a greenish hue and very rough. The turtle Is classified scientifically as "festudo lyra." 
 When angered the turtle spouts like a whale and threshes the water into foam. It is believed that a school of these turtles has been carried here in some ocean current. The steamer Santa Cruz, which came into port today, captured nearly a dozen smaller specimens in the channel this morning.”
headline: "HUGE TURTLE IS TO GO TO FAIR"
notes: "'festudo lyra' = testudo lyra, a historic name for leatherbacks; four feet in width and from tip to tip of flippers is about 10 feet; article also notes almost a dozen more smaller leatherbacks were caught a few days later in the same area"

text:
"William J. Forbes' Boat Upset Near Ensenada and He Struggles for Two Hours In the Water

 SAN DIEGO. Oct. 29.—Word has just been received from Ensenada of the narrow escape from death of William J. text: "A 700-pounder. \n This morning, as the U. S. Coast Survey steamer McArthur was steaming from her late anchorage in Beecher’s Bay, Santa Rosa Island, toward the coast, a large turtle was descried just astern of the ship, lying in the water breast upwards. It was apparently disabled, as was then supposed, by the ship’s propeller. Those who were below decks were surprised by the sudden order of “hard-a-port!” and as they rushed on deck, to inquire why, were soon shown the immense specimen swimming off, showing its head every now and then as it came to the surface to breathe. The ship was heeded directly for it, and the dingy made ready to lower, one of the men, who professed to be a great turtle-catcher, in the bows ready for the attack upon the monster. The ship having approached to within a short distance of the object of its travels, the headway was checked and the boat was lowered. A few strokes with the oars brought the dingy to close range, and when the turtle came up to breathe, over went the man, landing astride the turtle's back. No doubt the reptile was surprised, for its surprise was evinced by its diving under the boat, carrying with it its unwelcome rider. It was a question whether to sink or to dismount, so our friend chose the latter alternative, coming to the surface blowing like a porpoise, while the turtle made off with its utmost speed. The boat followed in its wake, which could easily be distinguished by the broken water. A second dash was made, and again a third, but without avail. Meanwhile, whenever the opportunity offered, rifle shots were fired from the ship, all missing the mark. The chase became very exciting, especially as upon the fourth attempt the turtle showed signs of fatigue, diving under the boats without attempting to make off. Finally the ship approached and as the turtle rose to the surface to breathe, a rifle shot from the forecastle ended its career. The boat then ran alongside the turtle, and making a line fast to its flippers, towed it to the ship. The task of preparing it to hoist on board was no small one, as the turtle was immense, and not being quite dead was continually opening and closing its huge jaws. Eventually it was hoisted on board by the fall of one of the boats, and laid on its back on deck. It was the largest specimen ever seen by any one on board, weighing probably in the neighborhood of seven hundred pounds. One of the rear flippers was gone, although the accident had not been of late occurrence. This probably accounts for its inability to make better speed through the water. It was a female of the hawk-bill species. It had evidently been stunned by contact with the ship or the ship's propeller, as the monster’s head was bruised. The measurements taken were as follows: From the tip of the nose to that of the tail 6 feet 6 inches; from the tip of one fore flipper to that of the other 8 feet; around the breast 7 feet 10 inches. The McArthur came into port this afternoon with her immense prize."

"Legends of Peninsula Say Old Tortoise Alejandro Was Tamed by Selkirk. 
 Old Alejandro has been captured alive, away down south of San Quintin, and now lives ignominiously upon the floor of the San Diego Fish company’s market at the foot of D street. 
 Alejandro, the pet turtle of Robinson Crusoe, according to the legends of the Mexicans of Lower California, has been the terror of all fishermen since the whaling days, and so tradition says, in the days of the whalers fought the whaling boats. Antedating the days of the whaling ships that sailed hence from the coast of Maine, the old turtle wrested for his domain with the Spanish galleons, gold laden, and Manila bound. 
 Many are the tales that the Mexicans tell their little children of the prowess of Old Alejandro, the turtle that knew no fear and that could sink a whale-boat with one stroke of his powerful flipper. Like the bugaboo of the northland, he would “get the little children if they did not watch out.” 
 They say that he was gentle once, several hundred years ago, when he followed Robinson Crusoe around the shores of Magdalena bay, although he is not mentioned in the historical accounts that tell of the presence there of Alexander Selkirk (Robinson Crusoe. It is a matter of history that Selkirk was at that time the second-mate of a British warship. 
 Legend following history, the folklore of the peninsula, is full of incidents in the life of old Alejandro. 
 He was captured two weeks ago, speared by an Indian fisherman many miles below San Quintin. 
 In company with two others of his kind, the famous old tortoise is awaiting the headsman’s knife and will soon round out his semi-millenium in a pot of soup on the range of a restauranteur."

Dr. Yates contributes the following account of the ocean turtle, classifying the Santa Barbara find: The curious reptile known by the name of turtles, or tortoises, are remarkable for the peculiarity of being a vertebrate animals Wi.a their bones worn on the outside of the lody. They are divided into several general classes with different habits and characteristics. The kind most valued for this product is the "hawkbill turtle,” which is found on portions of the west coast of Mexico; while the flesh of this turtle is not considered edible, its eggs are thought to be a great delicacy; the female fs very prolific, laying a large number of eggs at intervals of three weeks, which is also the period required to hatch the young. They are laid In the sand and hatched by the heat of the sun. When the hatched young have to run the gauntlet of many enemies before they reach the sea, toward which they instinctively rush. The writer has a specimen of the above species. The “green turtle” is the best known of the sea turtles. Its flesh is highly prized by epicures. The Jaw has two curved sharply pointed teeth, and the extremity of the lower Jaw is strongly hooped. The flesh is not good for food, as it causes many symptoms of poisoning in those who eat it It feeds on fish, and other marine animals, and lays about three hundred and fifty , eggs at a time. One of its best known hatching places is the Turtle Islands of Florida. It Inhabits the warm regions of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, and grows to a great size, often weighing more than 1600 pounds and attains a length of 8 feet From the great development of its fore legs, it ib a good long-distance swimmer, and often ventures far out to sea, and is sometimes driven to strange countries. text:
"Measures Over Six Feet in Length and Will Weigh More Than Six Hundred Pounds. 
 Landed on the Beach After a Terrible Struggle—Is Considered of Great Value—Will be Put on Exhibition—Exceptionally Good Eating. 
 Sebastian Larco is in possession of a large turtle caught by his men yesterday afternoon, which is considered to be worth hundreds of dollars to a museum or institute. 
 Every afternoon about 4:30 o’clock the fishermen in his employ pull in their nets, which are set in the channel about a mile and a half out. Yesterday, while they were returning, they noticed several large splashes resembling a whale in distress, located in the center of the kelp. They immediately turned their boat in that direction, and on arriving at the spot noticed that the cause of the disturbance was a monster turtle, caught in the kelp and unable to extricate itself. After considerable hard work a rope was fastened to it and an effort made to bring it into the boat. Finally the monster was dragged in,  but scarcely had it been landed before it struck one of the men with its wing, or fin, sending him headlong into the ocean, and then crawled back into the water. 
 The fisherman succeeded in getting back into the boat again, and, regardless of his wet condition, set about to securely fasten the rope to their prize. A terrible struggle ensued, the monster of the ocean fighting viciously for freedom, and the two men working to prevent him from doing so. 
 At last the work was accomplished, but it was considered better not to again attempt to land him in the boat. The rope was securely fastened and the turtle towed to the beach and landed. 
 A wagon was called and their capture was safely landed at Larco’s residence. Then another struggle began. The turtle objected to being taken into the fish house, and three powerful men were unable to master him. They were thrown aside by the turtle, carried upon his back and occasionally thrown down. More assistance was needed, and not until six men with ropes attached to the monster’s body were they able to conquer him. 
 Captain Larco was interviewed by a representative of The Press and his account of the capture was as follows: 
 “The boys have secured a great prize. It is a pure green turtle, and of great value, not only as a curiosity, but its meat is of the finest quality. During all my experience of almost half a century, I never heard of but one other being captured on the Pacific coast. It was taken by government officials aboard the survey boat McCarty, near San Francisco, many years ago. I should judge that the one captured by the boys weighed about 1000 pounds. They do not as a rule enter shallow water, but live thousands of miles at sea. It was a great surprise to me when I saw it.” 
 The exact weigth of the turtle is not known, yet it will weigh over 600 pounds. IT measures almost seven feet in length by four feet across the back, and from tip to tip of the front fins over twelve feet. 
 Mr. Larco will exhibit it, beginning tomorrow. An effort will be made to have it put in the bath house, where thousands of people could see it. By throwing salt water over it daily, it can be kept alive indefinitely, and no doubt a large price will be offered for it by some museum. 
 Captain Alexander of the Santa Rosa was at the dock when it was brought in, and will ascertain its value when he reaches San Francisco. 
 Plano Larco and Pietro Marfolli were the fishermen who captured it.”

text:
"Thousands of Persons Fascinated by Display of Marine Oddities 
 More than 150,000 persons have visited the Marine Museum at Cabrillo beach to marvel at the varied specimens of ocean life on display. 
 In San Francisco today visitors from all sections of the world gape at a replica of a monster turtle --- a 1,100-pound giant of the sea --- the original of which was a gift to the local museum. 
 It is said to be the largest turtle ever caught and brought from tropical waters to these shores. Thirty-five years ago a turtle weighing slightly less than 1,000 pounds was caught and brought here. This was the only other time a turtle, even approaching the size of the recent catch, was landed in this section. 
 Today the replica of the monster not only is one of the features of the exposition’s aquatic show, but also the center of interest at the local museum, where a duplicate plaster cast appears. 
 The Cabrillo beach museum provides a place where persons interested in the nature lore of the Pacific coast may learn about the flora and fauna of the sea and shore and also bring in their own private collections of birds, fish, shells, and other specimens for identification. 
 From this beginning the museum has grown until it now contains hundreds of fascinating specimens of the under sea and shore denizens of the Pacific. 
 Many strange varieties of fish found in waters off the coast of California, Mexico and tropical islands to the southward are on display, as are preserved iguanas, Galapagos turtles, birds and rare creatures of many varieties seldom seen by the casual visitor to the sea shore. 
 The giant sea crabs, many varieties of shell fish, specimens of plant life, snakes, and a great variety of other creatures are also displayed, many of them in settings depicting their natural habitat. 
 Growth of the museum has been assisted through donations to it by various expeditions to Mexico, Central and South America, including those of Captain G. Allen Hancock, well known sportsman-explorer. The museum is under the direction of Dr. William L. Lloyd, former University of Pennsylvania naturalist. In addition to serving as curator of the institution, Dr. Lloyd conducts many nature study hobby groups for both children and adults at the municipal playgrounds of Hollywood and Los Angeles."

text:
"The giant sea turtle named “Malintzin” cried without words, crying so that Carlos Boccaccio couldn't eat one bite of her. 
 Carlos used to own a restaurant in Tijuana, where sea turtles are a standard delicacy. This particular “Tartatuga” weighed 300 pounds, and was about to be put to her death, when large tears formed and dropped from her eyes. 
 Carlos, the gourmet, saw this; saw this creature without words making her final protest to something she didn’t understand, and he never tasted her fine meat. 
 Other turtles, yes. 
 Both before Malintzin and since. 
 Even we have savored turtle soup that Carlos has made, and hope some day to taste turtle liver saute, turtle steak, salad, scaloppini, and all the other dishes the animal is noted for, even vitamin oil. 
 “Malintzin” carries the Aztec name of the princess who married Cortez. She was caught by a Mexican fisherman in warm Baja waters and sold to Carlos. She, and all others like her, was kept alive with wet sacks covering her reptile back. And like all others, she preferred Baja waters because of its warmth and also because she was isolated there. 
 She was ashore digging a hole and laying her eggs when she was captured. Her eggs weren’t disturbed, so her babies would be able to take to the sea ten weeks later when they learn to swim well, 25 miles an hour like their mother could. 
 They will probably hear about their 225 variations of relatives, all the way from the tiny turtle in the pet store to the giant tortoise. 
 And they too will probably forget all words of caution and land ashore on a warm, isolated beach to lay their eggs. 
 Perhaps fishermen will be there again to flip them onto their backs so they cannot get away and take them to market. 
 Then again there will be more steaks, soups, sautes and vitamin oil."
headline: "The turtle cries with big tears"

text:
"A National City man, Ludwick Egger, could hardly believe his eyes when a giant sea turtle surfaced near his boat while he was fishing in San Diego Bay this week. 
 “I never heard of sea turtles around San Diego,” he said, “but there he was.” The turtle surfaced about 50 feet from the boat the first time he was spotted and later surfaced about 35 feet away, Egger said. 
 Egger said he had a fishing companion in the boat, “and he can vouch for the turtle.” Egger, who lives with his wife at 43 L Ave., said he is taking a ribbing from friends who insist he saw the turtle because he was intoxicated. 
 Egger said he saw the “big flippers” of the turtle “and I got so hungry. I dearly love turtle. Those big flippers make wonderful roasts.” 
 Egger said he is concerned about the turtle causing a speedboat accident “My grandson has a speedboat, and if he hit that big fellow it would wipe out the boat” 
 A member of the San Diego Zoo’s Reptile division staff said, “Although it is certainly not an everyday occurrence, sea turtles do get up this far north. I have heard of four or five instances where turtles were sighted in the bay.” 
 The turtles weigh from 200 to 800 pounds and abound in the southern waters."

"A sudden flareup of dirty water slowed up yellowtail fishing at the Coronado Islands last weekend, but it appeared to be clearing rapidly early this week and good fishing for the July 4 weekend appeared to be in store. 
 When the slow-down occurred at the Islands, the La Jolla and Point Loma kelp beds quickly took up the slack, and anglers had little difficulty fattening their sacks with barracuda, and calico bass, plus some white sea bass and yellows. 
 Among National City anglers who switched to La Jolla and hit the jackpot were V. C. Daniel, who limited out on barracuda, and G. Tweed and L. Tweed. Charles Phillips stuck to the Coronado Islands through thick and thin and was rewarded with a 22 pound 5 ounce yellow. 
 Before the dirty water moved in, anglers made daily catches of from 258 to 501 yellows, and veteran rod and reelers expected similar catches once conditions are back to normal. 
 Most unusual catch of the week was the taking of a 1000 pound leatherback turtle by anglers aboard the Red Wing last Friday. First take of albacore, 18 of them, was made the same day by Ray Ward and Ben Burch, aboard the Channel Clipper, one hour south of the Coronado Islands."

text:
"Two car loads of San Diego county products left for St. Louis yesterday, consisting of fruits, vegetables, minerals and grain of as fine a quality as can be shown from any county in the State. Ensenada sent her quota from Baja California, among which was an immense living sea turtle, with which the Bay of Punta Banda abounds. 
 At Fallbrook the cars will be reinforced with two living full-sized ostriches in full feather, grown without irrigation. While many of the fruits may not stand transportation, and arrive in as good condition as when sent, there will be sufficient to base a proper opinion on what this heretofore neglected country can do comparatively with others, whose boom commenced and died down to a legitimate condition long before ours was generally known to exist. 
 Our Grand Army Corps, who have taken this portion of the St. Louis exhibit in charge, know our important responsibility as representative men. 
 Mr. Wm. Lyons accompanies the procession, and what he lacks in exhibit can be made up with his, “literary specials’’ and placer gold samples, with which he is well provided. 
 Several representatives of our local press will be in St. Louis, and many of our other citizens, all of which will have a tendency to give San Diego a satisfactory representation, and prove that such men as Lyons, Large, Hartzell, and others, were not propagated and brought to their present condition on climate alone; and after exhibiting themselves they can exhibit their rations. When the late Professor Louis Agagssiz remarked at a public assembly that that the climate of San Diego would produce a fortune to each of its then 2500 inhabitants there were but few that then appreciated the prophecy. Some 20,000 people have come to this city alone within fifteen months, and come to stay with us, while the county at large has been filled up in proportion. 
 R. W. Dana in his phenomenal experiences with the Wide Drayers in 1834 and 5 reports San Diego as then the only port of safety on the “northwest coast.” characterizing about all others as the hell holds of California. 
 Mrs. Helen Jackson in her “ramona,” written from personal observation here, pays a continual tribute to the climate and its productions, and speaks of a special suburb as “Oneonta,” or the place of rest. It’s a mottled question whether the “Oneonta” known to the trade and now sold in 25x140 lots has been proselyted to that purpose. Mr. Peck, of “Peck’s Sun,” even excels Mrs. Jackson in proving up the resting qualities of our climate. He relates that he came here to hunt and fish, but while enjoying a day’s rest previous to this hunting, he found resting was the very thing to do, and kept at it while here. In his last letter from Riverside to his paper he opens it with, “The old gentleman is still resting.” Mrs. Maria Burton, widow of General Burton, U.S.A., in her narration of the “Don and Squatter” from 1872 up to a recent date, confirms all previous statements as to climate that the radical element of emigration failed to interrupt. Our real estate agents of to-day keep up the refrain and in many instances seem to emulate the historic “Silas Megg” and “drop into poetry” without meaning to plagiarize. At the same time there is nothing abnormal in the condition of San Diego."
headline: "SAN DIEGO BEGINNING TO BOOM"

"E.S. Hoyt Has Negative of a Rare Curiosity—Photographs Furnished to Academy of Science 
 E. S. Hoyt is the owner of a kodak negative of rare value. Prof. F. M. Anderson of the Academy of Science of San Francisco has sent here to have some photographs developed from this negative from which wood cuts will be made to be used in embellishing a write-up soon to be printed. The subject of the photog[r]aph is a mammoth turtle captured in Santa Barbara in 1901 and seen by Mr. Hoyt at that time when he secured the negative while the huge animal was on a pair of trucks. 
 It will be remembered that a monster turtle was captured in the waters off the coast of Santa Barbara last summer. The two turtles were alike, the latter being somewhat the larger, and are the only two of the kind ever captured in California waters. Neither lived and it happens that Mr. Hoyt has the best negative known to exits of the first turtle. 
 Some of the pictures were finished yesterday at the Lewis gallery and sent to the Academy of Science. The matter being prepared for the writeup will doubtless be of considerable value and interest as the turtles were monsters and of a very rare species."

text:
“Dr. L. G. Yates has Charge of the Interesting Work. 
 THIRTY-FIVE FEET OF STITCHING 
 Will be on Exhibition in Some up Town store in a Short Time—Monster Curiosity. 
 Unless something happens mighty quick, the big turtle which was captured by Larco in the channel last month, will not know himself at the resurrection. For the past four days Dr. L. G. Yates has been engaged in mounting the monster. A representative of The Press called on the doctor yesterday. Aproned and bloused, he was stitching away, closing the last seam in the turtle’s hide. There is something like 35 feet of stitching on the monster’s body. 
 In a few days the work will be completed, the eyes put in to give it a more lifelike appearance, and the former inhabitant of the briny deep will look complacently on the moving crowd from some up-town window. He has already been treated to a most remarkable diet, one that will last him for some time to come. Dr. Yates was just ramming home the last charge of dessert yesterday. It consisted of a generous stepmother supply of excelsior. Previous to that course he had been treated to a full meal of blocks, hay, straw, boards and several pieces of wagon-tire steel. There is nothing delicate now about the appetite of the turtle. 
 The skin has yet to be treated with stains in order that it may retain its natural color. Then it will be varnished, and the head poised at the proper angle. The specimen will be one of the most interesting caught in the waters of the western coast.”

“Inscription Cut in Shell,' “E. J. W., El Dorado, 1858,” Creates Interest. 
 [LOCAL CORRESPONDENCE] 
 VENICE, March 6. — An aged sea turtle was caught off the Venice breakwater today. On its back was the following inscription: "E.J.W., El Dorado, 1858.” 
 The lettering was etched deep into the tortoise shell and must have been done many years ago. What the name “El Dorado” signified can be left to anyone’s imagination. It may be the name of some ship that sailed the southern seas in the days of the ‘49‘ers, or it might mean merely a name carved by some sailor without any special purpose. 
 The shell was badly damaged in getting the turtle ashore. so after some vain speculation by the fishermen, the creature was tossed back into the ocean.”

text:
"Weighs Eight Hundred Pounds, Is Eight Hundred Years Old, Comes From California. 
 [DIRECT WIRE TO THE TIMES.]·
 NEW YORK BUREAU OF THE TIMES, July 30.—[Exclusive Dispatch.] One member was added today to the "zoo" family in the Central Park menagerie. The newcomer is a large leatherback turtle, said to be one of the largest in captivity. It weighs 866 pounds, measures five foot, six inches from nose to the tip of tall and three feet, six inches across the back. 
 Benjamin Katzenstein presented the turtle to the park department. He says it was caught in the Pacific Ocean off the California coast, and it is one of the deep sea species. 
 Katzenstein pointed out sixteen squares on the turtle’s back and said that each of the squares represented fifty years of life. This would make the turtle 800 years old."

“SEA MONSTER WEIGHING ALMOST TON IS CAPTURED 
 On Its Shell Is Discovered Inscription Showing That the Animal Had Been Captured by British Sailor in Southern Seas Twenty-six Years Ago. [BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS— P.M.] 
 SAN DIEGO, June 21.—One of the puzzles of the sea came to the surface yesterday, when a gigantic turtle was captured by Julius Solissa, a fisherman in whose net it had become entangled. The monster weighs 1902½ pounds, or almost a ton, and its shell is five feet two inches from tip to tip. On its back, somewhat plainly, is burned or carved this inscription: 
 “British ship Sea Bride, August 12, 1881. 8 south, 86 west. If found please notify Thomas Fletcher, Brawley Road, Rivington, England." 
 It would appear from this that the turtle was captured twenty-six years ago in the South Pacific and that he was released after the lettering had been burned in its shell.”

“GIANT TURTLE IS TAKEN ON MALIBU COAST. 
 Threat of One Relative Against Another Follows the Preliminary Examination of Figueroa, Accused of the Murder of His Bride—Orators Train for High School Contest. 
 SANTA MONICA, June 1-From the mystic Malibu coast has come a giant sea turtle that, according to some scientists, must have been celebrating the one hundredth anniversary of its birth about the time the three wise men were searching for the Star of Bethlehem. Those who profess to know something of the life and habits of these strange creatures of the deep arc authority for the statement that this monster could not have been less than 2000 years of age. This turtle was of the leather-back variety and weighed 1500 pounds and is said to have been one of the largest ever captured. It came from near the mouth of Corral Cañon, seventeen miles from here, and was discovered on the beach by William Campbell. 
 The monster was alive when Campbell was passing along the strand. It had evidently been washed in by the tide and was probably sick, as but little resistance was offered by it. The thing was killed by beating its head with a rock. The flesh was cut away and the great shell, six feet long and almost five feet across, was preserved. The flippers were three feet long.”

“FISHERMAN TRIES VAINLY TO GET IT IN PORT ALIVE. 
 Monster Seven Feet Long and Believed to Be Thousand Years Old. Second One of Species Ever Captured Off Coast Kills Itself in Struggle for Freedom. 
 SAN PEDRO. July 17.—After trying for two days to tow into port alive a big turtle of rare species, Steve Williams, an East San Pedro fisherman, arrived home this morning, but the monster was dead. The turtle became entangled in a buoy rope attached to his nets, and ropes were made fast to its flippers. Had not the engine of Williams's launch become disabled, the turtle would not have killed itself in its efforts to regain its freedom. 
 It is the second of its kind ever captured in these waters and weighs about 1000 pounds. It is estimated that it was 1000 years old. It was more than seven feet in length, and measured nearly nine feet between the extremities of its front fllþpers. 
 Unlike the land turtle, It has two long front flippers and two short hind ones, like those of a seal. The shell is soft, with five ridges down the back. Fishermen occasionally see turtles of this species in the fishing banks, but say they are very timid, and that a boat cannot get close enough to capture them. This one was caught in twenty fathoms of water. 
 Williams will have his prize mounted and sell it to a museum.”

text:
“CHELONIAN REPTILE CAPTURED FROM A LAUNCH. 
 Record for Deep-Sea Turtles Broken by a Catch of Fifteen-Hundred-Round Creature—Age Calculated at Between Two and Five Centuries. 'Tis a Reg’lar Festudo Lyra. 
 [SPECIAL CORRESPONDENCE OF THE TIMES.] 
 SAN PEDRO, May 8.—San Pedro seems to be able to hold its own in the matter of deep-sea monsters Just a year ago George Evich interested the scientific world by bringing to this port over half a ton of turtle caught by him in the launch Bell. Today Jerry Marincovich went Evich one better and captured a 1500-pound crustacean in his nets off Catalina Island. The desperate attempts of the huge crustacean to escape resulted in its death, and it is now on exhibition at the Morgan Oyster Company in this city. 
 The turtle captured by Marincovich today is undoubtedly the largest crustacean ever captured and hundreds of people today have marveled at its size. Its age is estimated at between 200 and 500 years. 
 The turtle belongs to the species Festudo lyra, or "Sphargis mercavialis," these names having reference to the myth that the shell of some turtle was used by Mercury in the construction of the lyre. This family is Chelonian. 
 Before Evich’s capture a year ago the largest marine turtle ever captured was taken in the Galapagos group of islands several years ago and was taken to London. It weighed 850 pounds and was known to have been over eighty years of age. It was still growing at the time of its death. 
 The age of the turtle taken today is a matter of conjecture, but his corrugated coat of mail full of the knocks of time would indicate that he had existed for several centuries. 
 The Chelonia family of turtles possess a tail but no teeth. Jaws are provided with a horny sheath with hard and sharp edges, forming a beak like a parrot’s Marine turtles are spread over the equatorial and subtropical seas, and sometimes stray beyond these limits, being seldom taken above San Diego 
 The Chelonians are diurnal animals and only a few of the family are active during the night 
 They are extremely quick in the water, either to seize their prey or to escape danger. The marine turtle periodically migrates to breeding stations. The species inhabiting temperate waters hibernate 
 The marine turtle possesses great tenacity of life, surviving injuries to which other reptiles would succumb in a short time. The heart of a decapitated marine turtle will beat many hours after every drop of blood has been drained from the body and the muscles of the trunk and head show signs of reflex action twenty-four hours after the severing of the spinal cord. 
 Some marine turtles are herbivorous and others carnivorous their prey consisting of fish frogs and other aquatic animals The limbs are modified into paddles by means of which they propel themselves through the water with extraordinary rapidity, but are unfit for locomotion on land, where their progress is as awkward as that of a seal The toes are enclosed in a common skin out of which only one or two claws project. 
 The catch made today by Marincovich is important from a Scientific standpoint on account of the great size of the monster. 
 The carapace is seven feet long and six feet wide and the weight is easily 1500 pounds. The monster will be mounted and sold to some museum.”

“Large Santa Barbara Turtle and Its Captors. 
 Capt. George Gourley and Albert Stafford of Santa Barbara caught a monster sea turtle in the ocean near the pleasure wharf of that city Tuesday. Still alive the big animal specimen was hauled to the pleasure wharf and made fast with ropes. Its estimated weight is 800 pounds. 
 Stafford first saw the turtle while rowing in a small skiff. It was entangled in seaweed and seemed to be asleep. Stafford went ashore and found Gourley and the two put out in a sailboat. The managed to gaff it in one of the flippers and throw ropes about it so they could bring it to the pier. The turtle made fierce resistance. 
 According to a classification of Prof. Dodge of the High School of Santa Barbara the monster specimen is a Sphargis coriacea, or leather-backed turtle. When it was hauled to the wharf there were a number of small fish known as remoras attached to it.”

 —San Diego Union Staff Photo. 
 Holding up two pilot fish attached to the back of a 50-pound sea turtle they caught off Coronados are Carter Mahrdt, 11, and his brother, Clark, 13. 
 Two Encinitas boys got a bigger thrill out of their first deep sea fishing trip yesterday than they had anticipated. 
 Clark Mahrdt, 13, and his brother, Carter, 11, went out seeking yellowtail and ended up with a 50-pound sea turtle. 
 The brothers set out at 2:30 a.m. for the Coronados with their father, Wiliam Mahrdt, a masonry contractor, of 215 Vulcan Ave., Encinitas, and Hollis O’Hanlon, of 2004 Coast Blvd., Del Mar, in O’Hanlon’s 35-foot boat, the Boxer. 
 They began fishing with live bait about daybreak. 
 O’Hanlon said they were having very little luck when the turtle took the boys’ bait about 9 a.m. The hook caught in the shell of its mouth, and the boys managed to get it to the side of the boat. The skipper and their father brought it aboard. 
 Attached to the turtle’s shell were two pilot fish. 
 “The boys got more of a thrill from the turtle than they would have from a dozen yellowtail," O'Hanlon declared. 
 He said the youngsters’ eyes were popping and their mouths were agape when they brought the catch close enough to the boat to see what it was. 
 “We thought it was impossible,” declared Clark. 
 O’Hanlon said the turtle was about 500 miles north of its regular territory. “They very seldom come this far north,” he said. 
 The catch attracted a crowd of onlookers when it was landed at Pitcairn Marina on Shelter Island, where O’Hanlon’s boat is moored. 
 The men said they planned to contact the Scripps Institution of Oceanography to see if officials there have any use for the turtle.”

“[image included] Crowd inspects captured 750-pound turtle on freight elevator. Charles Sweeney, at left, and Billy Cromer, second from right, are among seven sailors who caught it. At right is Arvid Roper, U. S. Grant Hotel chef who gave it temporary home. 
 LARGEST IN CAPTIVITY 
 By JOE BROOKS 
 A 750-pound turtle last night reached the comparative tranquility of a commercial aquarium near Palos Verdes after some harrowing experiences in the San Diego area. 
 It is the largest turtle on exhibit anywhere. And if it remains alive, it will be the first Leatherback turtle that ever did so in captivity. 
 If not, it'll make a mammoth pot of turtle soup. 
 The turtle's bad luck started Sunday when it ran afoul of a boatload of seven U. S. sailors while loafing in a kelp bed off Rosarito Beach. 
 TWO-HOUR STRUGGLE 
 The sailors were imbued with that natural human instinct of catching anything big that one encounters. They lassoed the critter with the anchor line and after a two-hour struggle succeeded in getting it ashore and hoisting it into their car trunk. 
 On the trip to San Diego the weight of the huge reptile broke the car springs. Then on arrival, no one could be found to take custody of the creature. The zoo couldn't. The city pound wouldn't. 
 The sailors finally left the turtle in the basement of the U.S. Grant Hotel. Sam Hinton, curator of the aquarium at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, placed it [t]emporarily in the quarantine tank at Scripps. 
 "There were four of us and we nearly killed ourselves getting that turtle moved," Hinton said. 
 TOOK 10 MEN 
 Three men from Marineland Aquarium arrived in a pickup truck late yesterday afternoon to take the turtle there. 
 Ten men lifted it out of the tank and placed it on its back on a mattress on the truck bed. 
 A cargo net was used to truss it for the trip north. 
 Leatherbacks are the largest species of turtle, Hinton said. But none has ever lived in captivity, "although this one looks like it has a good chance," he said. "It is in good shape." 
 "We'll put it in the porpoise tank," said Frank Calanbrino, assistant collector at Marineland. "People love to see those big lumbering things swimming around."”
headline: "Monster Turtle Survives Ordeal"

text:
“[image included] A 243-pound turtle was posed for his picture yesterday afternoon after he had been speared from Mission Beach bridge by B. M. Hill. It is estimated that the monster denizen of the sea was in his prime about the time the Declaration of Independence was signed. Standing behind the turtle to the left is W. W. Roberts, superintendent of the Neptune Sea Food company, who bought the catch from Hill (right). The spear which Hill sunk into the turtle’s neck is shown. 
 Catch Weighed 243 Pounds; Its Final Form Will Be Turtle Soup on Epicures’ Table 
 Just 243 pounds of potential turtle soup was enjoying; a personally-conducted sightseeing tour of Mission bay yesterday afternoon when he met with bad luck in five prongs. Today the huge turtle, one of the biggest caught near San Diego in many years, is residing temporarily in a private tank owned by the Neptune Sea Food company. He doesn’t know it, but in a short time he will be in many little cans and will be labeled as "Sapphire Green Turtle soup stock.” 
 Whether the denizen of the ocean was attracted to San Diego by reports of the far-famed climate here, or whether this is only one of several ports he intended to make on an extensive vacation trip, is a matter for speculation. At any rate he was probably far from home yesterday afternoon when B. M. Hill’s spear sank itself in his neck under Mission beach bridge. The turtle lives—or most of his kind do—far down the coast of lower California at a place known as Turtle Bay. 
 The unusual visitor in San Diego yesterday measured four feet from the tip of his nose to the end of his shell. W. W. Roberts, superintendent of the Neptune company, estimated that the turtle was between 300 and 400 years old. Two men standing on top of his shell apparently caused him no discomfort. 
 Hill, who lives at 85 Third street, was on the Mission beach bridge spearing for halibut and shark yesterday afternoon, when he saw the monster turtle swimming under the bridge. ”Just to see what the turtle would do.” Hill hurled his spear. His aim was perfect, as the prongs dug into the reptile’s soft neck. If the spear had hit the shell it would have glanced off, blunted, Hill believes. 
 It was manifestly impossible to lift the huge creature over the rail on the bridge, so Hill had to tow it to the beach, which was no easy task. All four stout flappers of the turtle were brought into play to oppose Hill, and it resolved into a fight of muscle and wit. Hill won, after a half hour of struggling. The turtle was dragged up on the beach and turned over so he couldn’t crawl away, then lifted into Hill's machine, in which it was carried to the plant of the Neptune company, at the foot of Juniper street. 
 Turtles of the size of the one caught yesterday are rarely found in San Diego waters, according to those who follow waterfront occurrences. 
 When a Union photographer called on the turtle to take his picture yesterday the prisoner was still in Hill's automobile, and had to be removed from the machine and deposited on a truck to be placed in the sunshine. The turtle took a lively interest in the proceedings and appeared not to thoroughly approve of them. He waved his flappers around menacingly as he was being dragged from the automobile. No sooner was he safely landed on the truck than he tried to scramble off. When deposited on the scales to be weighed, the turtle persisted in resting two or three flappers and part of his weight on the floor, with utter disregard for the kind of “story” he would make for the papers. Finally he was turned over on his back. 
 Late last night the turtle was resting easier in a small swimming pool of his own filled with salt water. There he will await the arrival of a French chef from Los Angeles, who will make soup out of him. Even the shell probably will be used, as it contains gelatine which will thicken the soup stock.”

text:
“Union Photograph of 1175 Pound Turtle Brought to Port Yesterday. This Turtle is Said By Waterfront Men to be the Largest Specimen Ever Caught In Lower California Waters. [image included] 
 Appearance of Shell Leads Fisherman to Believe Marine Giant Nearly 200 Years Old and Probably Come From Tropics. 
 A huge turtle, weighing 1175 pounds, was brought to port yesterday morning by Captain J. Zollezzi, of the Italian fishing launch Belvedere. The turtle, said by waterfront men to be the largest specimen ever caught in Lower California waters, is nine feet in circumference and seven feet from the tip of its nose to the end of its short tail. The front flippers are four feet in length and almost a foot wide, tapering gradually until at the end they are about five inches wide. 
 The jaws are a solid mass of teeth, over 200 being located in the upper jaw. They range from one-half to a quarter of an inch in length. The shell is ribbed and in spots pliable, which leads many fishermen to believe that the turtle is nearly 200 years old. The lower part of the jaw is streaked with gray. 
 Captain Zollezzi reported that the turtle was captured after a terrific struggle five miles off Cape Colonet on the Lower California coast. The turtle became entangled in Zollezzi’s fishnets, and before it could be extricated about $50 worth of fishing gear was destroyed. 
 C. Y. Wiley and M. Mose are seen in the photograph holding the turtle’s front flippers. Wiley believes that the sea reptile originally came from the Galapagos islands, below the equator, as the turtles in those waters are noted for their enormous size. The turtle will be placed on exhibition today at the American Union Fish Company’s plant at the foot of G street.”

text:
“Percy Woods and the men who assisted him to land mammoth turtle caught in kelp beds off the harbor, showing size of crustacean as it lay on the beach. 
 [image included] 
 Battle Four Hours in Attempt To Land Huge Crustacean Weighing Half Ton 
 After a four hour battle, lasting from 1 o’clock yesterday afternoon until 5. Percy Woods, a fisherman in the employ of the San Diego fish market. Landed a huge tortoise, weighing half a ton, perhaps the largest ever seen on this coast. When first sighted by Woods, who was lobster fishing off Point Loma, the monster crustacean was entangled in the kelp just outside the harbor and was fighting furiously for its liberty. Every movement entangled it more seriously in the treacherous kelp and had relief not so opportunely offered. it would undoubtedly have succumbed. 
 With great effort, the turtle fighting every second, Woods succeeded in passing a rope around its body just behind the front flippers, and then cut loose the kelp twined about the turtle’s head and body. Starting the engine of his boat he then proceeded to tow the captive into port. The turtle resisted, but because of its inability to exert much strength in a backward direction, it was unable to stop the forward motion or the small gasoline schooner. Had Woods fastened the line behind the rear flippers, and attempted to tow the turtle into port backwards, it would easily have been able to turn the tables, probably carrying the fishing schooner to sea. 
 As it was, it took Woods four long hours to reach the wharf of the San Diego Fish market, at the foot of D street, with his prize. Here, however, he met with further trouble. Transferring the rope to a small skiff, he thoughtlessly began to row ashore, thinking to tow the monster behind him. Finding that it was to be again put into motion, the turtle resisted and turned around, making for deep water. The skiff was dragged helplessly along, Woods’ efforts to the contrary being in vain. Finally fishermen on the wharf, sizing up the state of affairs, threw Woods a line, making one end fast to the wharf. 
 Fights to Last Ditch 
 Six or eight men working at the market fastened themselves to the rope, and their combined effort? were necessary to haul the skiff with the struggling turtle to the shore. Here the turtle was dragged out on the beach and walked around to the front of the market. Half a dozen men holding the rope were unable to retard its progress when it desired to continue on its way. the only means of controlling its action being to turn the head and keep the monster walking in a circle. 
 The turtle was finally brought to the interior of the market where, before a crowd of curious onlokers, the rope was fastened to a workbench by C. E. Osborn, the manager of the fish market. The turtle, however, was not satisfied with its position, and promptly began dragging bench and all away from the wall to the opposite side of the big room. The rope was rapidly untied and hitched around a post supporting the roof. When this, too, was torn from its position, one of the men got busy and bored two holes in the floor, one on each side of a stout joist. The rope was then passed around this and the monster was finally secured. 
 Manager Osborn is undecided what disposition to make of the big reptile, and in the meantime it is occupying the spot light on the floor of the fish market. The turtle measures eight feet in length over all, is forty-two inches across the back, the surface of the upper shell being twenty inches from the ground. It is thought to be of the species known as the loggerhead (capuana carcita), in rare instances seen in this section of the Pacific and easily the largest ever captured on the Southern California coast. It weighs about 1000 pounds. 
 Shell Peculiarly Marked 
 The shell of the tortoise is a peculiar one, being marked with six rows of protuberations. One of these lines each side of the shell, the others occurring in regular intervals to the center of the shell and running lengthwise, speculation as to the age of the monster is rife. Tortoise have been known to live 100 years or more. and it is believed that the species to which the captured one belongs retains its hold on life for a much longer period. 
 One of the rear flaps has been completely cut off, supposedly bitten by a shark. The other rear flap is several feet in length, while the front flaps are fully three feet long. 
 The shell of the tortoise is considerably marked and scratched, some apparently of recent date, while others may have been inflicted many years ago.”

text: “Yesterday Smith Warren, A. J. Werner and Misses Alice and Grace E. Marvin of Los Angeles chartered the launch Twilight, Capt. W. H. Graves and while trolling off Point Vincent sighted a monster turtle, which Graves says was nine feet across, with a head like a barrel. The Twilight ran alongside and Graves drove a harpoon into it, but the monster did not linger and disappeared with the harpoon which had a red handle. The party spent the remainder of the afternoon chasing that red handle all over the channel, but failed in their attempt to lasso it. Graves had a Winchester on board but no cartridges. Fishing parties now have an added attraction presented them of chasing a red handle stick whenever they see it, with the knowledge that a turtle weighing over a ton is anchored on the other end of it.”

text: “MAMMOTH TURTLE. \n On the return from the whistling buoy to San Pedro breakwater, a huge turtle was closely passed. The commodore got the pikepole ready as the yacht was swung around for the encounter, but the huge beast did not wait for the tourney and disappeared. This turtle was caught the same night in the nets of the Italian fishermen and brought into San Pedro the next morning, where it turned the scales at 1600 pounds and was sent to the St. Louis Exposition as a California product. It probably came, however, from more southerly islands and seemed to be of the same species which Darwin found!\ in the Galapagos Islands, and which he described in his "Naturalist's Trip Round the World.” This species attains great age and size, is possessed of much sugacity and makes long ocean passages from one island to another. text:
“E. W. Scripps of San Diego, who, with his family and party of friends, in two yachts and a power launch, were in the bay here a week ago, are now sojourning at the Isthmus, and will probably remain there for the next two months. Mr. Scripps has just chartered two more boats here, the yacht Avalon, and the fishing launch Mero, and they went up to the Isthmus this morning. The outing is taken for the benefit of the health of one of Mr. Scripps’s boys, and the family is accompanied by a tutor, a physician, a secretary and a storekeeper, besides servants. They will use the Avalon for making trips to San Nicholas and perhaps other islands of the channel group. They are out for a good time, and expense cuts no figure. The party is well pleased with the Isthmus, and they are negotiating for a lease of the Barracks and the cottages near by. 
 D. J. Alberga, with the Pacific Coast Biscuit Company, had the honor of bringing in the only big fish today. He got a 195-pound black sea bass, which kept him out of mischief for an hour and a half. A picturesque feature of his catch was when his boatman, “Shorty” Bencke, skipper of the Catalina, finding the fish was about to carry the line into his propeller, jumped overboard without divesting himself of his clothing and diving under the boat prevented the fouling of the wheel and saved the fish! With Mr. Alberga were M. E. Conboy and F. J. Matthie of Tucson. 
 The launch Idlewild took a party to the Isthmus. The trip was arranged by Mrs. L. J. Merritt for the members of the Moscos and Cosmos Clubs of Pasadena and their friends on the island. The party consisted of Mrs. L. J. Merritt, Mrs. George Kelly and Mrs. J. H. Farley of Stanford; Mr. and Mrs. Ammerman of Duluth, Mr. and Mrs. Earl Barnhart of Chicago; Misses Alice Ammerman, Daisy White, Evelyn Merritt, Bertha Merritt, Daisy White: Messrs. Horace White, John Newkirk of Berkeley, W. Arthur McNally and Mr. Newberry. 
 F. L. Hober, W. H. and Harry Bollyn ran up against a fighting shark this morning. They were out for sand dabs, of which they made a good catch, and were coming home, trolling a line for yellowtail, when a white shark about four feet in length took the bait. He fought hard till they got him up near the boat, and then he made a lunge for them, and came near landing in the boat. He made several more tries at it seeming determined to get at them, when one of the men clubbed an ore and dispatched the vicious brute. 
 H. T. Kendall of Pasadena, who now has the honor of holding the word’s record for biggest fish, has method in having the monster 419-pound fish mounted. He is vice-president of the Potter Hotel Company at Santa Barbara, and proposes to give the big bass a place of special honor in the hall or lobby of the new hotel, which is the largest lobby contained in any hotel in the United States, which makes it appropriate that it should contain the largest fish. 
 Capt. Trefethen of the Hermosa reports having seen an enormous sea turtle yesterday on his trip over from San Pedro. It was not more than a hundred feet away from the track of the vessel, and he had a good view of the creature, which he asserts was from eight to ten feet across the back. The captain says this is the largest turtle he has ever seen in his experience of more than twenty years in these waters. 
 The Mascot took out a fishing party yesterday, composed of Miss Carrie Connell of Phoenix, K. C. Kitt of Tucson, Misses Corinne Frances, Celia Knowles, Leota Latimer, G. Campbell, W. Culver and A. Cooper of Los Angeles, who caught seven yellowtail and three barracuda. 
 James Burton Adams, editor of the Denver Post, with his wife, is again visiting Santa Catalina. Mr. Adams says they design taking up their residence in Los Angeles at no distant day. 
 Mrs. Helen Safford, who has been here the guest of Mrs. Ed Stanton for a fortnight, left for her home in Los Angeles this morning regretted by a large circle of friends. 
 J. A. Simpson, master mechanic of the Southern Pacific Railway at Los Angeles, accompanied by his wife, is taking an outing on the island for a week. 
 Miss Sylvia Bowman of Pasadena and Miss Mabel Leaverton of Hollywood, are guests of Miss G. Myrtle Stotts at Beach Haven cottage. 
 Maj. H. C. Eggers of Fresno joined a number of his townsmen and friends at the Grand View for a few days.”

text: “Among the fishermen outside yesterday in the choppy sea were two young men from San Diego, who had great sport catching a school of sea turtles into which their smack happened to run. The turtles were upon the surface of the sea, sunning themselves, and floating lazily along. The boys rigged up strong lines with nooses, and stole silently alongside the biggest fellow, who seemed to be asleep. With a quick jerk one of his flippers was caught, and the rope jerked taut. \n There was a lively sequel, and the big turtle pulled himself together and tried to dive. He could not, and reappearing, he started on a fast gait to the southward. The toys gradually hauled him to the gunwale, where with another line they got him into the boat. He weighed 276 pounds. In this manner they caught thirteen big turtles, running from eighty to 245 pounds. It is not often that the turtles are found off this part of the coast, as they prefer the warm water of the Gulf of California. \n The fish catch yesterday was: Halibut, 100; lobsters, 150 pounds, trout, 100, croakers, 175; silver smelt. 135 pounds.”
