text:
"Competition Established in Lobster Importing. 
 New Deal Below Line Giving Hope of Lower Cost. 
 Big Fines for Trout and Quail Law Violators—Turtle. 
 Competition in Lower California fisheries, so earnestly advocated by the Fish and Game Commission as a means of increasing supply and thereby lowering prices to fish consumers, set in with a most business-like rush yesterday. 
 Two boats came into San Diego yesterday with load of lobsters, and the three concerns now operating below the line expect to average five tons each per week once they get into action. This will mean fifteen or more tons of lobsters coming into market in place of less than five, and local dealers believe the price cannot be longer monopolized by anyone so there is a chance hereafter of the general public getting a taste of this delicacy which heretofore has been the special prerogative of the rich. 
 Sunday night Deputy Pritchard took two inspectors, to San Diego, who are commissioned to go south with the boats of the importing concerns, who hold permits from the Carranza government. These officers are paid by the importers as required by law, and their duties are to certify that the provisions of the California law governing lobster importation are respected. A third inspector has been asked for by the 10th of April. 
 In addition to granting permits overriding the concessionaires operating for the de facto government of Lower California, President Caranza has taken the California fish and game laws for his guidance in conserving the West Mexican fisheries, and has appointed his own inspectors to accompany the boats of his concessionaires to see that they take no young fish, use no trawlnets or other gear destructive of the future supply. Carranza has taken the ground that much of the ablest fisheries thought and study available has been spent on the California fisheries conservation problem, which is very similar, and instead of merely patterning after it, has adopted it in toto. 
 Work of the concessionaires under this new competitive arrangement fostered by the simplifying of importation under rulings of the Fish and Game Commission, will extend to the fresh-fish trade as rapidly as they can get organized for it. Owing to the distances to be traveled, fast boats with refrigeration are essential to bring up the halibut, which so far have been caught mostly by San Pedro and San Diego fishermen on a 2 cents ??? [scanned newspaper is illegible] ???  … cents more has been added, so the Los Angeles trade have had to pay an average of 8 cents, and the freight. By the new arrangement the Carranza concessionaires will combine several of these profits, and prices to the public can be materially reduced. The supply is said to be greater than California ever had, and the feeding banks are better. 
 The territory is divided among the Carranza concessionaires, and the floating cannery John C. Heston is now in Magdalena Bay working on turtle and oversize lobsters until the albacore began to run, when she will go to putting up tuna. Lobsters of legal size will be inspected, boiled and shipped to California in cold storage, as the distance is too great to bring them in alive: but live shipments from closer points are now being made. 
 The former controllers of the Lower California fisheries had an eighty-foot yacht bought presumably for patrol purposes, but she is tied up in San Diego under the Federal order denying clearance to any transferred vessel for foreign ports because of international complications. The former patrol boat Ensenada is tied up without a crew since the memorable “battle of the halibut banks” wherein some poachers decoved her close aboard then rammed her, chasing her ashore. 
 This has been a week of much action and big fines in field patrol circles, trout “sooners,” six of them, falling victims to Deputy James II. Gvger on San Jacinto reservoir for snagging “spawners”. They had fifteen fish in their car weighing forty-five pounds and a Riverside justice imposed $25 fine on each, or $150 for the day’s fishing. 
 At the same time, Deputy Tipton Mathews served a warrant on a last year’s quail case, wherein two men now in Taft were arrested for exceeding the quail limit in Monterey county and placed under $100 bond each. 
 Late advices from San Diego are that three boats have come in with lobsters from Lower California this week and another is due the 4th of April. Besides lobsters, these boats brought in seventy turtles from 100 to 200 pounds each, which will swell at 8 cents a pound in Los Angeles. This is not as cheap as it seems owing to the great waste; only about one-third is usable, but the meat is rich and delicious."

 A Turtle Turn—The Delights of Turtle Eggs—Catalina Rowers Surprised—The Yellow Tails Still to the Fore. 
 Avalon (Santa Catalina Island), Sept. 6.—[Special correspondence of The Times.] A party from the Hotel Metropole were rowing around the point south of the hotel near Pebble Beach yesterday, when a curious round head popped out of the water, and a low hiss broke the stillness. One of the party was sure that it was a sea serpent; another thought it was something no one had ever seen before; but the head belonged to a fine green turtle, a big fellow, that would have tipped the scales at 500 pounds at least, and if turtle soup is not served at the hotel this week, it will not be the fault of the fishermen, who are camping on its trail night and day. 
 Several of these reptiles have been seen about Catalina this summer, and it is supposed that they have been ashore, certain curious marks on the beach that puzzled the finders being laid at their door. If this is so there was a nest, and as out of any batch of turtle eggs laid a goodly per cent fail to change into young turtles, there must be some eggs there yet. 
 Several parties have been out scouring the sandy beaches, and all sorts of trails have been followed up and worked in vain. The green turtle, in the experience of the writer, is fond of strolling on the sands on moonlight nights, and if by any chance the big fellows decide to come in there will be some great sport, and perhaps the would-be turtles would like some pointers from an old hand at the sport, who has “turned” a good many, and been laid out if not knocked out. 
 On the last green turtle party it was my good fortune to attend, there were four or five ladies, so that six or seven couples were made up, and by 9 o’clock, just as the full moon was rising we were stationed all along the sandy beach of an island about one-fourth as large as Catalina. 
 Every few moments the gentlemen of each party would start out and patrol the space between each other, walking rapidly along near the water watching for tracks. We did this for half an hour, when I noticed two tracks leading up from the water. 
 Following them up on a run I almost stumbled on a big green turtle, busily engaged in throwing the sand out of a hole. The moment she saw me she turned, and shouting for help I seized her by the shell, and lifted. I raised her about a foot, then her big flipper came swinging around, filling my eyes full of san and almost knocking me over, while she went rapidly toward the water. Three of us caught her again about half way down and with a piece of board, tried to turn her, but not until the fourth man came, did we succeed in turning the largest green turtle I ever saw. They do not bite, but for throwing sand and scraping gravel, they beat the world. 
 The turtle season to the south of here is in May or June, and what the big fellows are doing in shore now, when they should be in the high seas, is difficult to determine. 
 La Paloma, Hancock Banning’s yacht, picked one up on her trip down from San Diego, and probably the one that has put in an appearance around Acalon will be caught. 
 The fishing for the past week has been the best of the season, and is being enjoyed by large numbers of Los Angeles people. The summer rush is over, and ample accommodations are to be had by those who do not like the crowds of the mid-summer time. The Metropole has a delightful society of its own, about a hundred guests being there, many families having taken rooms for the month of September, which promises to be the gayest of the season. Admission day is to be celebrated here in fine style, a yacht race, tub race, pig hunt, swimming match and various diversions being arranged for. 
 The Hermosa makes a grand excursion around the island with a band, and the Wanda and Hartie have arranged for special excursions to the various points of interest. 
 The yellowtail fishing which started in so furiously the first of the week has kept up, and every day good catches have been made. 
 Mr. Sumner is arranging for a grand goat hunt at Middle ranch, in which a number of Los Angeles sportsmen will participate.”

“Turtles on the way to San Diego to be transformed into turtle soup, turtle meat and turtle oil. Top picture shows one section of confining pen at Scammon’s lagoon, with a number of the prisoners; middle, schooner Catarina, which brings the turtles here, aground on the shore of the lagoon. Below, loading the turtles on the Catarina. 
 Fishing for turtles is the interesting work of George Naylor and his brother William, sons of E. H. Naylor, 1904 Atlantic street, and Richard Johnson, all of this city. While interesting, the pursuit of turtles from 100 to 400 pounds is the hardest kind of work, as well as being extremely dangerous. 
 The Naylor boys and Johnson are under contract with the Lower California Canning company of National City to supply turtles, and they make their catches In Scammon’s lagoon, 400 miles south of San Diego. 
 Methods used in turtling differ, but the local boys use a net strung over about 1200 feet of water, the lower part anchored to the bottom and the other on the surface, buoyed by corks. This net is strung across the channel used by the turtles in going to and from their feeding grounds in shallow water. The turtles are approached while feeding and are frightened towards the net, where they become entangled In the meshes, which are about a foot in width. 
 Wherever a turtle becomes caught, the corks on the surface are pulled under, and the turtles, in rowboats, pull in the net and land the turtle in the boat. Considerable skill is necessary to accomplish this part of the work, for in many cases the turtles are much heavier than the man in the boat. 
 From the rowboats the catch is transferred to a motorcraft which lands the turtles on shore. A specially constructed pen, capable of confining hundreds, next receives them, and there they remain until the schooner Catarina arrives. 
 The Catarina is chartered by the turtles and makes from two to three round trips a month between San Diego and Scammon's lagoon. Upon the Catarina's arrival at the lagoon the turtles are brought from the pen to the motor boat and thence to the school. Great care is necessary during the transfer, and, despite all precautions, many of the turtles escape. 
 Two of the three partners remain on the turling grounds all the time, one of them making the semi-monthly journey on the Catarina. On arrival of the catch here the work of canning the meat and soup and extracting oil from the shell and fat of the turtles begins. The size of the Catarina’s cargo varies from 15 to 30 tons, and, while the craft is away on the trip to the cannery, the work of refilling the confining pens at Scammon's lagoon goes on unceasingly. 
 The turtle canning Industry is a comparatively young one here, as the Naylor boys and Johnson started only three months ago. shortly after their return from the army. The investment of the partners amounts to more than $10,000. The cannery also represents a considerable investment.”

“Steaks and Soup Put Up by Packing Concern; Supplied By Three Boats. 
 San Diego has a new industry. It is the canning of green turtle steak and turtle soup. The plant is located near the foot of Thirty-second street in the buildings formerly occupied by the Lower California Chemical company for the manufacture of aniline dyes. 
 The National City Commercial company, headed by J. K. Blackman. has taken over the Lower California Chemical company’s property and converted it into a turtle canning plant. A number of retorts for cooking turtles have been installed. Apparatus for making 800 gallons of turtle soup at a time also has been placed in the plant. 
 The turtle cannery is supplied by a fleet of three boats. Two ocean-going launches are employed in capturing turtles in Scammell’s lagoon, just south of Ensenada. The power schooner Catarina brings the turtles to San Diego, making three voyages a month. The Catarina arrived from the south last week with 45 tons of live turtles and is now at Scamell’s lagoon loading another cargo. 
 The products of the turtle cannery will be distributed throughout the United Slates.”

text:
“SAN DIEGO soon will have the novel distinction of being the world's first turtle-oil exporting port. 
 According to word received here yesterday from the lower coast, a gang of Mexicans is employed in Scammell’s lagoon killing turtles from which an excellent grade of soap oil is obtained. 
 The lagoon is said to be fairly alive with turtles ranging from 75 to 200 pounds in weight. At one period recently the Mexicans had turtles piled up like cordwood waiting to be cut up and rendered for the oil. 
 The first shipment of turtle oil is expected here from Ensenada this month. The oil sells wholesale at $1 a gallon. 
 Shark oil also is imported here from the Lower California coast. This oil is utilized in the manufacture of cosmetics.”

"Sixty Per Cent of Investment in Southern California and Forty-four Per Cent of Total Values Created in Local Harbor. 
 Fisheries students long have marveled at the phenomenal growth of California’s sea food industries during the war; but figures just issued by the State Fish and Game Commission have an equally compelling interest for the general public. 
 Aided by the various enactments of the last legislature rendering all facts accessible concerning catches at their origin, and reinforcing them by requiring exact reports as to the pack, the fisheries statisticians have found that the preserving or fish alone has now gone considerably beyond the “Twenty Million a Year” class. Not counting the enormously growing fresh fish demand, now that Californians really have begun to take their fish more seriously as a food supply, the export fisheries business alone takes rank as a capital industry of the first magnitude on its showing during 1919. 
 The compilation shows that nearly eight million was invested in canning, drying, salting, smoking and pickling sea products giving employment to no less than 8242 persons. This harmonious combination of capital and labor swelled the wealth of the state by the splendid total of $21,417,743. 
 Southern California again led the state, and took rank as foremost center of production by contributions to this total of, respectively 60 per cent or $12,294,064 and 44 per cent or $9,694,482. The spreading sphere of the truly excellent California sardine in the world’s markets is attested by its pre-eminence in the total pack, surpassing even the "sea chicken” already so well set up on a gastronomic pedestal of its own by the albacore tuna canners. 
 Many species none too generally known in their fresh state, have been packed in varying quantities, some experimentally, others on such substantial basis as Monterey’s 3538 cases of the toothsome and delicate squid, only properly appreciated by the Mediterranean peoples. The epicurean green turtle, celebrated of bou-vivants the world over, figures to the extent of 7407 cases, the “raw material” having been imported from the sandy strands of Lower California bays where the turtles come ashore to deposit their eggs. 
 Evidences of constant effort to add something to the food of the world are abundant in the fisheries compilation of 1919, suggesting general appreciation among the canners of the great truth that because it can, eventually the sea must feed the land. Packers of fish are embracing new products at a rate that speaks well for the building of an immense direct export business of canned sea foods from the ever-widening harbors of the south where produced, to those foreign peoples who already have learned to laugh at the meat barons through mastery of preparation, and appreciation of the food value of fish. 
 When the figures on last year’s fresh fish business are compiled by the Fish and Game Commission, it is predicted upon the information already tabulated, that some more and bigger surprises are in store. While it is true that Californians as yet have not fully learned to eat fish, the figures make it apparent that they are rapidly learning. High meat prices, war premium upon every nature of food supply, and the wide advertisement given sea products by state conservation authorities played their part, but the genuine excellence of the Pacific Coast fish themselves when properly prepared is really doing it. Housewives are gradually learning that a fine fish is worth as much culinary attention, and as loving preparation as they would lavish upon a choice roast or fowl, or a piece of game. Foreign cooks learned that lesson long ago. The ready cooked products of the cannery, scientifically and deliciously prepared, have created considerable taste for the fresh product also, and the combination bids fair to go towards solving the present high cost of living by diversifying the present top-heavy demand upon meat, potatoes and a few other over-exploited staples. 
 Despite the enormous tonnages represented by the figures, and notwithstanding the multiplication of canneries with capacities of 150 tons per day, the State fisheries experts insist that the possibilities of California’s marine resources are but scarcely scratched, as yet. Aliens make constant use of dozens of species little understood by Americans, fully equal to many in daily use, and superior to some. At present rates of increase, the astonishing totals of today’s fisheries business in another decade will seem trivial. Intensive methods, scientific preservation, elimination of some present wastes, are all along the trend of present times."

text: “SAN PEDRO, June 21. — [Regular Correspondence.] The prospect of establishing a cannery here for the packing of the sea products of the Lower California waters is favorable, according to S. W. Waring, late manager of the Catalina Conserving Company’s lobster-packing plant in this city. Mr. Waring returned Tuesday from a trip down the coast about one hundred and twenty miles beyond the Mexican line. Turtles of a kind very like the much-prized green turtle of commerce are there in abundance, and the transportation of them for packing at this port seems to be practicable. The turtles, which average about one hundred and twenty-five pounds in weight, and some of which weigh as much as 200 pounds, may be caught in shallow water. The natives capture them with the use of spears, but that method would not do for turtles to be brought here. They may be taken unawares by men wading in the water and approaching them when asleep. A quick little motion by hands grasping the lower edge of the shell on one side turns the turtle on its back, and it is then practically helpless. The turtle is made ready for transportation by tying its fins and placing a block of wood so that the head may not fall too far down and cause strangulation. Waring says he has shipped live turtles treated in that manner from Galveston, Tex., to New York city without injury to them. If the number of turtles brought to a cannery hero should be greater than could be used for a few days, they may doubtless be kept alive as long as desired in an in-closure in the bay. \n Eight kinds of meat may be obtained from the turtles, and from one of them weighing 125 pounds the edible parts weigh nearly one hundred pounds. In the same waters lobsters are plentiful and barracuda are abundant during the season when they are not found in such large numbers in the waters near here. There is no import duty on live or fresh fish taken in Mexican waters and brought into the United States, provided they are brought in boats of not less than thirty tons’ net register. If the fish bo in any manner preserved there is a duty of ¼ of a cent a pound imposed.”

“ONE OF THE FEW GREAT LAND-LOCKED HARBORS. 
 Large Enough to Handle the Traffic of New York or London Without Congestion—its former Commercial Glory Was Destroyed by Scientific Researches. 
 It may be said of Magdalena Bay, as it has been said of men, that some achieve greatness and some have greatness thrust upon them. This recess in the coast of Lower california, comes in the latter capacity. 
 The glory of Magdalena Bay prior to the time that this government thought of purchasing it, and later finally established it upon the map by deciding to coal its fleet in the spacious harbor, rested upon orchilla. This product comes from a desert plant and is valuable because it supplies the violet in the manufacture of dyes. When it was gathered and made into bales it used to sell at Magdalena for $1 a hundred, while upon arrival at Liverpool the market value had grown to $20 a hundred. These were palmy days in Magdalena, and the luxuries of many continents found their way into the little village, and the export duty brought much revenue into the coffers of the Mexican government. Twenty vessels were often seen lying in the harbor awaiting a cargo, and life in the village showed much activity. Then a chemical process was discovered for the making of the violet dyes and the industry fell off and the town shrunk within itself. 
 Magdalena Bay is the only deep-water harbor and perfect shelter from storm on the long barren coast of Southern California. It is one of the few great harbors of the Pacific Coast, and compares favorably with the bests in the world. Located in the vast solicitudes of a forbidding and unproductive coast, it is of such proportions that it could handle the traffic of New York or Liverpool without congestion. 
 SEVENTEEN MILES LONG AND TWELVE MILES WIDE. 
 The bay proper, exclusive of shallows, lagoons, and tributary inlets, is seventeen miles long and twelve miles wide inside of the five-fathom line, or the depth of thirty feet, which would be safe anchorage for the biggest ships. There are 130 square miles of this safe anchorage ground, ranging in depth from [3 or 8–clipping scan is illegible]0 to 120 feet. 
 The mouth of the harbor is between headlands that come close enough together to force the continued cutting of a deep channel but are still far enough apart to admit a flying squadron coming abreast. The vessel drawing the greatest water of them all would have yet forty feet to reach before her keel ground in the sand. Immediately inside the headlands there is twenty-two fathoms or 132 feet of water, the depth being such that it is not favorable for anchorage. The favorite anchorage is Man-of-War Cove, to the north of the mouth of the harbor, where protection is to be had from the winds by the rocky range of peaks that form the tongue of land which incloses the bay. 
 Farther to the north of these anchorage grounds are lagoons that are navigable far into the interior, but the channels of which are uncertain. The venturesome whalers who formerly inhabited these waters often push forty miles to the inland, following these lagoons, and returned with fresh water, and turtles as large as a roll-top desk. To the south there are shallow bays and a chain of islands run brokenly up and down the coast. 
 Back of all of there is the flat and sandy coast, parched by eternal suns and rainless. Farther toward the interior are cactus-covered hills and soil tudes that extend 115 miles without habitation to La Paz, the nearest settlement. On the tongue of land that cuts off the ocean is the village of Magdalena. Sheer above it rise the rocks that shield it from the storms, but offer neither vegetation nor fresh water. The village sits at the base of these mountains on a level strip of land from which the water depth drops off in such a manner as to allow small boats to land direct. A wooden pier extends half a mile into the bay, and is accessible to all classes of boats. 
 In the village of Magdalena are twenty-five houses and fifty inhabitants. The houses are some of lumber but mostly of adobe, and cluster around the customhouse, which is the center of the village. Here an individual with the title of judge and captain of the port also officiates as customs officer and wields authority over a stretch of land hundreds of miles in extent, but with no more population than the number of his neighbors in the village. His chief duty is to hang a lantern at the front door of his dwelling on nights when a vessel is expected, and collect duties on the orchilla exported. 
 With only one entrance, safe and wide, but easily defended, the great natural harbor of Lower California is declared by naval experts to be the finest station in the world for a naval base, and by far the best harbor on the western coast of North America. The right to use it as a coaling station, and for the rendezvous of the United States Navy, was the concession secured by Secretary of State Root from the Mexican government. 
 When the Panama Canal is opened Magdalena Bay will serve as a valuable strategic base from which American warships will protect the Pacific end of the waterway from invasion. 
 The topography of Magdalena Bay is ideal for the purpose to which it is now to be adapted, and the physical conditions are as perfect as could be desired. The bay itself offers an expanse of over 100 square miles of water in which the deepest draft ships can navigate with absolute safety. Opening into the bay from the lower end is another smaller bay, and to the north is a series of lagoons extending nearly 100 miles northward. Ships have navigated the lagoons forty miles up from the bay. The mainland shore of Magdalena Bay is of low, sandy loam, very fertile in places where water can be secured, and barren as the desert otherwise. Mexican ranches have, in recent years, sprung up all over the inland near the bay, and cattle and sheep are being raised. 
 The bay proper is seventeen miles long. Its approximate general depth is about seventeen fathoms, with an area of over 100 miles outside the five-fathom line. the battleships will have abundant room for practice maneuvers. A navigable channel connects the southeastern end of the bay with another large bay, called Almejas Bay, but dubbed "‘Leaward" Bay by mariners. This bay will not be navigable for warships, but it is a great source of revenue for the natives, furnishing literally millions of green turtles each year, which are edible: and are sent out by the shipload to Pacific Coast ports There turtles are considered a great delicacy by epicures. 
 A PERFECT CLIMATE 
 Oysters, clams and mussels are found in great abundance. The land surrounding the lagoons to the north of the bay abounds in curlew, ducks, and other game birds, and deer are very numerous and easily shot. 
 The climate of Magdalena Bay is perfect. Although located in a tropical latitude, ?? [clipping scan is illegible for about one paragraph] ?? which American war vessels can make a quick dash up the Pacific Coast to protect any of the coast ?? which may be in peril. Magdalena Bay seems to have been made by nature with that purpose in view. From the bay to the American boundary line is 600 miles. To San Francisco 1000 miles. Fast war vessels can easily make the trip between Magdalena Bay and San Francisco is two and a half days. Constant communication is maintained between Magdalena Bay and San Diego, by wireless telegraphy. 
 The entrance to Magdalena Bay is about two miles wide, very deep, and free from hidden dangers. Entrada Point, on the tip of which is a dome-shaped hill about 200 feet high, connected with the mainland by a narrow strip of sand and rock but a few feet above high water is the northern gate of the entrance. The southern gate is Cape Redondo, a round, rocky headland nearly 100 feet high, the land rising from it rapidly to a height of 841 feet at a distance of one mile, and 1691 feet at five and a half miles. Cape Redondo is the upper extremity of Santa Margarita Island, which forms the lower of the two great encircling arms of land which reach out and form the bay. Within a bend on the inside of the peninsula, which extends downward from the upper end of the bay, is located “Man-of-War Cove,” where the coaling station will be located in all probability. Here the shore is so steep that steam launches can land passengers dry shoed directly on the shore. 
 The regular boats from San Francisco to Panama stop each month, once on the up and once on the down trip. An occasional tramp or whaling vessel puts into the harbor for safety from storm, but the quietude of the place is rarely broken. It is doubtful whether Magdalena yet knows that she is to be visited by the greatest fleet that ever cruised the Pacific, and doubtful whether she will awaken from her apathy when she learns the news. 
 HOW THE BOATS WILL COAL. 
 The port will be enriched beyond her hopes of recent years by the coming of the fleet. Each vessel that enters the harbor must pay dues to the amount of $2.20 per foot of draft. With the entire fleet in the harbor, supplemented by the colliers that carry the coal and the various other vessels that will follow or precede the fleet, this amount of harbor dues will be such as materially to affect the prosperity of so small a village. 
 The manner of coaling in Magdalena Bay will be by means of the colliers. There are no dock facilities there that could handle the coal for the warships, and the harbor will be of benefit merely as offering a suitable place easily to effect its taking on. It is even doubtful whether fresh water will be obtainable, as the village is supplied by a boat that goes forty miles up the lagoons to a spring and returns to dole out its supply grudgingly. There are nearer springs to be found, but the water is brackish and unpalatable. The whole scheme of things is such as to offer but a magnificent deep-water harbor with no existing facility to supplement its attractiveness. 
 Should the United States acquire Magdalena Bay, as has been recently proposed, she would have the facilities for one of the greatest coaling stations on the Pacific Coast, and located at a point between Panama and San Diego that might be of great strategical value. Should it be bought at a price commensurate with its productive power, based on present performance, the price should not be such as to guarantee an increase in the tariff schedules. With sufficient advertisement, however, the bull market in bays might be such that Magdalena would sell much above par and bring no inconsiderable price in the open market.—Washington Post.”

“Father and Son Testify They Were Ill-Fed on Trip. 
 Get Judgment Against Owner of Coasting Vessel. 
 Dollar-a-month Contract is Branded as ”Doctored.” 
 The brine of the Pacific, beans and boiled turtle meat, the last named procured in the hot sands of the Magdalena Islands, formed the principal ingredients in the dish set before U. S. Commissioner Long yesterday, in the trial of the admiralty case involving the claims of Albert G. Stebernaler and his son. A. G., Jr., against A. H. Moore, owner and master of the gas schooner Newark. 
 Slebernaler, Sr, sued for $318.50. said to be due as wages as second cook on the vessel, and the commissioner gave him a judgment for $198 50. Theeboy asked for $326 50, and he was awarded $206. The commissioner figured that the defendant Moore should be allowed two months to make the trip from the Magdalena Islands to Acapulco, Mex., and back to San Diego, and that he should pay the plaintiffs for the balance of the time, the voyage requiring from April to November, 1919. 
 Slebernaler and the boy went to the Magdalena Islands to make assays for an amalgam corporation. Involving the deposits of manganese. It was expected that the Newark should call for them and bring them back to the United States, as the vessel had been utilized to carry provisions to the islands. But the vessel was delayed. 
 When the two got ready to come back to this country they found themselves without funds and the testimony showed that they went before the American Consul at Manzaniello. Mex., Harry L Walsh, and signed ship’s papers binding them to serve on the Newark, that later on touched at the island, until it returned to San Diego or Los Angeles Harbor. The Siebernalers found it necessary to work their way back 
 SUM PUT IN LATER. 
 The ship’s papers show that the two men, aged 46 and 20 years, respectively, agreed to work on the boat for $1 a month, but both witnesses said that figure had been inserted after they had signed the agreement in the office of the Consul That was where the argument started. 
 In the bill of complaint the elder Slebernaler sued for 165 days’ pay at $2 a day, as second cook on the Newark and the boy asked for the same rates as engineer for the same period. 
 The father gave his testimony some months ago, and yesterday the son was on the stand. He said that both had been compelled to work hard, and that the most of the time they were compelled to subsist on beans and turtle meat, but the witness admitted that Capt. Moore ate at the same table and had the same food. Both testified that they were ill-fed, were compelled to go without shoes, and the son said that he suffered from sore feet for a long time after the Newark reached her home port at San Diego. 
 Young Slebernaler stated that it was one of his duties to get up at 3 o’clock in the morning and go to the Mexican villages to get milk for Capt. Moore, and in addition he had to do the ordinary duties of a seaman, wash down the deck, etc He testified that Capt. Moore told him that his services were very satisfactory. Both the father and son thought a dollar a month was not enough for such work. But both denied that they had agreed to work for that amount, although the ship’s papers showed their signature to the agreement calling for the payment of the sum. 
 The judgment rendered by the commissioner will act as a libel on the Newark”
